[0] A cybersecurity regulator says tech giants need to do more to combat sextortion, singling out companies like Apple, Meta, and Google for failing to do better.

[1] Victims of sextortion are often young, including children under the age of 16 …

[2] A typical sextortion attack involves an impersonator pretending to be of a similar age to the victim, who flirts online. At some point, the attacker sends a nude image they claim to be of themselves and invites the victim to reciprocate.

[3] If the victim does send a photo back, the attacker threatens to share it publicly, often claiming that copies will be sent to their family and friends via social media unless a ransom is paid to delete the images.

[4] TNW reports that Australia’s cybersecurity regulator eSafety says tech giants are not doing enough to detect these kinds of attacks.

[5] Taking Apple as an example, the regulator believes Apple should attempt to detect this kind of script sent via iMessage, just as it detects nude photos sent to children. The report also says Apple needs to make it easier for victims to report such attacks.

[6] The regulator says the problem is severe, with more than one in 10 teenagers aged 16 to 18 having been victims, more than half before they turned 16.

[7] 9to5Mac’s view

[8] The scale of the problem looks staggering, and there have been cases in which teenagers have taken their own lives over sextortion. I agree with the regulator that tech giants, including Apple, should do more to tackle this crime.

[9] iMessage messages are end-to-end encrypted. However, Apple’s existing technology for detecting nude photos shows that it is possible for the company to perform on-device analysis on the recipient’s device without compromising privacy. A similar approach could be used to detect these scripts.

[10] Apple may already be working on the issue. A developer has spotted a malicious-message detection feature in iOS 26.6 beta 5.
